metadata.repo_type_justification: Application source with a deployable entry point (src/claims_agent/agent.py main guard), a dependency manifest (requirements.txt), and single-service CloudFormation IaC (infra/agent-runtime.yaml, infra/agent-iam.yaml).
metadata.archetype_justification: agent.py coordinates a multi-step sequence across four downstream dependencies - Bedrock knowledge-base retrieval, AgentCore Memory read, Bedrock Converse, model-driven tool dispatch into the claims Postgres database, then a Memory write - with conditional tool selection. That is multi-service workflow coordination, not simple fan-out.
metadata.surface_flag_rationale: psycopg2 connection built from a Secrets Manager credential in tools.py (persistent data store); AgentCore Memory, the 3653-day transcript log group, and the claims database are at-rest surfaces; infra/agent-runtime.yaml provisions an AgentCore Runtime container and a Lambda (deployed, inherently multi-instance workload); the AgentCore Gateway exposes MCP tool endpoints (API surface); both templates provision AWS::* resources. IaC is application-scoped only, so SEC-Q1 is Not Evaluated.

classification.rationale: 5 High, 23 Medium, 5 Low findings. MOD classification is softer than ARA on a single High: in ARA one High is an agent-deployment gate, in MOD one High is typically a single modernization gap and maps to Pilot-Ready. Five High findings - public network exposure, no CI/CD, no encryption at rest, no staged deployment, no integration testing - place this service past that threshold. Score band 1.85 (Needs Work) and count tier (Remediation Required) agree.

top_gaps.title: Network Security
top_gaps.gap: AgentCore Runtime is NetworkMode: PUBLIC with no VPC, subnets, or security groups anywhere in IaC.
top_gaps.impact: The money-moving tool path has no network boundary; the gateway's assumed private subnet route is not backed by any in-repo network control.

top_gaps.title: CI/CD Automation
top_gaps.gap: No pipeline definitions of any kind - no .github/workflows/, buildspec.yml, Jenkinsfile, or CodePipeline in IaC.
top_gaps.impact: Every application and CloudFormation change is a manual deploy; no gate exists to enforce the remaining remediations.

top_gaps.title: Encryption at Rest
top_gaps.gap: No KMS key or KmsKeyId on any data surface - Memory, the 3653-day transcript log group, and the claims database all use default handling.
top_gaps.impact: SSNs, bank routing numbers, and full prompts/completions sit at rest for ten years with no customer-managed key or key policy.

top_gaps.title: Deployment Strategy
top_gaps.gap: Container deployed as claims-agent:latest with no traffic shifting, canary, or rollback artifact.
top_gaps.impact: A bad prompt or tool change reaches 100% of auto-claims triage immediately; batch-mode rollback is manual row reversal.

top_gaps.title: Integration Testing
top_gaps.gap: tests/test_tools.py is two mocked happy-path unit tests; no integration, contract, or safety-evaluation suite and nothing runs in CI.
top_gaps.impact: settlement_writer - which releases payment - has no end-to-end or adversarial test coverage before release.

detail.guard_satisfied: Data-processing workloads evidenced: nightly 500-claim in-process queue drain (docs/batch-mode.md) and full-claims-archive knowledge-base ingestion into OpenSearch Serverless (src/claims_agent/retrieval.py). Archetype is orchestrator, not stateless-utility or data-gateway, so the archetype exclusion does not apply.
detail.current_state: No SQS, SNS, EventBridge, Kinesis, or MSK resource in either template; no messaging client in requirements.txt; every triage hop is a blocking synchronous call; knowledge-base ingestion is undeclared in IaC and unfiltered per principal.
immediate_actions: Replace the in-process nightly drain with an SQS queue plus dead-letter queue consumed by the existing Lambda, so each claim is independently retryable.
Move multi-step triage coordination to Step Functions so each claim is a durable execution with retry and compensation rather than one long-running Python loop.
Define the knowledge-base ingestion as an explicit IaC pipeline over an S3 landing zone so corpus scope becomes a declared, reviewable property.
Emit settlement decisions to EventBridge so the system of record and audit consumers decouple from the agent's success path.

pathways.name: Move to AI
pathways.key_trigger_criteria: No AI/agent frameworks, no vector DB, no RAG, no agent eval framework (primary), gated on AI/agent/LLM intent in the repository
pathways.not_triggered_reason: AI intent is evidenced ('agentic', 'Bedrock', 'RAG', 'vector store', 'large language model' in README.md), so the contextual guard passes - but the primary trigger requires an ABSENCE of AI frameworks. Bedrock Converse (src/claims_agent/agent.py), langchain-aws (requirements.txt), a Bedrock knowledge base over OpenSearch Serverless (src/claims_agent/retrieval.py), and AgentCore Memory are all present. Only the agent-evaluation supporting condition holds (no Ragas/DeepEval or eval harness), and a supporting condition cannot trigger the pathway; that gap is reported under SEC-Q7 and OPS-Q6.

findings.title: Primary claims database consumed but not declared in IaC
findings.description: The claims database is reached through a Secrets Manager credential (CLAIMS_DB_SECRET default 'claims/db/readwrite') and a psycopg2 connection in src/claims_agent/tools.py. AgentCore Memory is a fully managed store. No self-hosted database is declared anywhere - no engine in a Dockerfile, Compose file, or Kubernetes manifest. The Postgres instance itself is not defined in this repo's IaC, so Multi-AZ and failover posture cannot be confirmed from in-repo evidence.
findings.gap: The primary production data store is consumed but not declared. Its management mode is inferred from the connection pattern rather than evidenced, and nothing in-repo pins it to a managed engine with automated failover.
findings.recommendation: Bring the claims database into this repo's IaC (AWS::RDS::DBInstance or an Aurora cluster with a Multi-AZ writer/reader topology), or add an explicit cross-stack reference to the template that owns it, so the service's data dependency is reviewable alongside the agent that writes settlements to it.

findings.title: Multi-step triage workflow hardcoded with no orchestration, retry, or compensation
findings.description: The multi-step triage workflow is entirely hardcoded in triage() in src/claims_agent/agent.py: retrieve comparables, recall memory, call bedrock.converse, loop over returned toolUse blocks dispatching into tools.REGISTRY, then write memory. No AWS::StepFunctions::StateMachine exists, no Temporal/Camunda dependency in requirements.txt, and no workflow definition file. No retry, no compensating action, no error branch - a tool failure mid-dispatch leaves the exchange partially applied, and docs/batch-mode.md confirms rollback is manual reversal of payment_queue rows.
findings.gap: Archetype-calibrated: because this service was classified as an orchestrator, the absence of orchestration despite genuine multi-service fan-out is the rubric's named anti-pattern for the archetype ('no orchestration despite fan-out - tight coupling and no retry/error strategy') and scores 1. The same evidence on a stateless-utility would have been recorded as Not Evaluated.
findings.recommendation: Model the triage pass as a Step Functions state machine with one state per dependency (retrieve, recall, invoke model, dispatch tool, persist), explicit retry and catch on each, and a compensating state for settlement_writer so a failed run reverses its own payment-queue row instead of relying on a human. Elevated priority: this is the archetype anti-pattern and it sits on a money-moving path.

findings.title: No managed messaging or streaming; synchronous-only fan-out across four dependencies
findings.description: No managed messaging or streaming resource exists in either template - no SQS, SNS, EventBridge, Kinesis, MSK, or Amazon MQ. requirements.txt carries boto3, psycopg2-binary, langchain-aws, and opensearch-py; no messaging client. Fan-out across Bedrock Converse, the Bedrock knowledge base, AgentCore Memory, and Postgres is synchronous and blocking. The 'nightly queue' in docs/batch-mode.md is an in-process loop over up to 500 claims, not a broker.
findings.gap: Archetype-calibrated: for an orchestrator, synchronous-only fan-out across 3+ dependencies scores 1 as a structural anti-pattern - cascading failure and timeout amplification. Had the archetype resolved to stateless-utility or data-gateway, synchronous-only communication would have been the correct design and scored 4.
findings.recommendation: Introduce SQS as the triage work queue with a dead-letter queue so each claim is an independently retryable unit rather than one item in a 500-iteration loop whose failure strands partially-applied settlements. Emit settlement decisions to EventBridge so downstream consumers are decoupled from the agent's success path. Do not add a self-managed broker.

findings.title: AgentCore Runtime deployed with NetworkMode PUBLIC and no VPC, subnets, or security groups
findings.description: ClaimsAgentRuntime is declared with NetworkConfiguration NetworkMode: PUBLIC, with the inline comment 'Public network mode so the adjuster UI can reach it from the corporate network without a VPC peering change.' Neither template defines a VPC, subnet, security group, NACL, VPC endpoint, or PrivateLink configuration. docs/security-review-TODO.md states the gateway 'sits on a private subnet route from the adjuster UI' - that route is not evidenced anywhere in this repository - and records that the runtime ARN additionally accepts SigV4 from any principal in the account, so the gateway is not the only path in.
findings.gap: No network isolation of any kind around a workload that reads SSNs and bank routing numbers and releases payments. The documented security model rests on a network boundary that does not exist in the provisioned infrastructure, and a second unmediated SigV4 path bypasses the boundary that was assumed.
findings.recommendation: Move the runtime to a VPC network configuration on private subnets, reach Bedrock, Secrets Manager, and the claims database over VPC endpoints, and attach least-privilege security groups so the tool Lambda is the only principal that can reach the database. Scope the runtime's resource policy so invocation is possible only through the gateway, removing the parallel account-wide SigV4 path.

findings.title: Managed MCP gateway present but with no authorizer, throttling, or request validation
findings.description: A managed entry point exists - AWS::BedrockAgentCore::Gateway ('claims-tools', ProtocolType MCP) fronting a Lambda target - but it is configured with AuthorizerType: NONE and the template sets no throttling, quota, or request-validation configuration. docs/security-review-TODO.md adds that tools/list returns the full registry, including settlement_writer, to every caller with no per-caller allow-list.
findings.gap: Gateway present with minimal configuration: no authorizer, no throttling, no request validation, and no per-caller tool scoping on an endpoint that exposes a payment-releasing tool.
findings.recommendation: Set an authorizer on the gateway (JWT/OIDC via a centralized IdP, or IAM), add throttling and request validation, and scope the advertised tool set per caller so a read-only adjuster session cannot enumerate or invoke settlement_writer.

findings.title: Scaling limited to untuned platform defaults with no data-layer protection
findings.description: Scaling is whatever the managed services do out of the box. The tool Lambda declares only Timeout: 60 - no ReservedConcurrentExecutions, no provisioned concurrency, no AWS::ApplicationAutoScaling::ScalableTarget. The AgentCore Runtime has no scaling configuration. No scaling policy exists for the claims database connection surface, and the batch path (--max-claims 500) is a fixed in-process ceiling rather than a scaled consumer.
findings.gap: Coverage is limited to implicit, untuned platform defaults, with nothing on the data layer and no business-metric-driven policy such as triage queue depth. Unbounded Lambda concurrency against a single Postgres instance is also a connection-exhaustion risk, since _conn() opens a new connection per tool call with no pooling.
findings.recommendation: Set reserved concurrency on claims-tools sized to the database's connection budget, introduce pooling or RDS Proxy in front of Postgres, and once the triage queue is a managed queue, scale consumers on queue depth rather than on CPU.

findings.title: No backup, retention, or restore configuration for any data surface
findings.description: No backup configuration exists in either template: no AWS::Backup::BackupPlan, no BackupRetentionPeriod, no point-in-time recovery setting, no S3 versioning, and no snapshot lifecycle policy. ClaimsMemory sets EventExpiryDuration: 365, which is an expiry (deletion) control, not a backup. The claims database - system of record for settled amounts and the payment_queue - has no in-repo backup posture at all, and no restore procedure is documented.
findings.gap: A workload that writes settlement decisions and releases payments has no declared backup, no retention definition, and no tested restore path.
findings.recommendation: Define backups for every data surface the service depends on - automated backups plus PITR on the claims database and an AWS Backup plan with defined retention - and document and exercise a restore runbook, recording results so the recovery path is evidenced rather than assumed.

findings.title: No explicit fault isolation; stateful dependency AZ posture undeclared and image tag mutable
findings.description: The compute tier inherits regional redundancy from AgentCore Runtime and Lambda, but no fault isolation is expressed anywhere: no subnet list spanning Availability Zones, no MultiAZ property, no cross-zone load-balancing configuration. The claims database's AZ posture is not visible in-repo. The runtime is pinned to the mutable claims-agent:latest tag, so a replacement task can pull a different image than the one currently serving.
findings.gap: Managed compute is implicitly resilient, but the stateful dependency's AZ posture is undeclared and fault isolation is not explicit anywhere in IaC.
findings.recommendation: Declare the database as Multi-AZ (or reference the template that does), place the VPC-attached runtime across at least two AZs when the network remediation lands, and pin the container to an immutable digest so instance replacement is deterministic.

findings.title: IaC covers compute and identity only; data, retrieval, network, and operational surfaces undeclared
findings.description: Two CloudFormation templates cover the AgentCore Runtime, Gateway, Gateway Target, Memory, tool Lambda, transcript log group, and two IAM roles. Four categories the service demonstrably depends on have no IaC here and are consumed by reference only: the claims Postgres database (a secret name in code), the Bedrock knowledge base and its OpenSearch Serverless collection ({{resolve:ssm:/claims/kb-id}}), the tool MCP endpoint ({{resolve:ssm:/claims/tool-endpoint}}), and the artifact bucket. The ECR repository is undeclared, and no operational or DR resources exist - zero alarms, dashboards, health checks, or backup plans.
findings.gap: Partial coverage: compute and identity are in code while the data, retrieval, networking, and operational categories are not. The SSM indirection hides the dependency graph rather than declaring it.
findings.recommendation: Extend IaC to the surfaces the repo exposes - database, knowledge base and vector collection, ECR repository, networking, and operational resources (alarms, dashboards, backup plans) - or add explicit cross-stack references and documented ownership for the ones provisioned elsewhere.

findings.title: No CI/CD pipeline definition anywhere in the repository
findings.description: No pipeline definition exists. Searched and not found: .github/workflows/, .gitlab-ci.yml, Jenkinsfile, buildspec.yml, appspec.yml, and any AWS::CodePipeline::Pipeline or AWS::CodeBuild::Project in infra/. README.md documents only a local pip install and python -m claims_agent.agent invocation. docs/security-review-TODO.md references a deploy role 'reachable without MFA from CI', so a CI system exists - but nothing about the build, test, or deployment of this service is declared or reviewable here.
findings.gap: Both tracks are unautomated in-repo: the application container and the CloudFormation templates are deployed by undeclared means, with no automated test, build, deploy, or rollback stage - and therefore no place to enforce the security and testing gates this report recommends.
findings.recommendation: Define a pipeline in-repo covering both tracks: build and push the agent image by digest, run unit and integration suites, run dependency and container scanning as blocking gates, deploy both templates through change sets, and provide automated rollback. Require MFA on the deploy role that can alter the agent, its model, or its guardrails.

findings.title: Clean module boundaries but two deployables share one artifact, credential, and IAM role
findings.description: One Python package, src/claims_agent/, with single-responsibility modules: agent.py (loop), tools.py (data/tool surface), memory.py, retrieval.py. Dependencies flow one way and there are no circular imports. The package is deployed as two independent units (AgentCore Runtime container and the claims-tools Lambda) from the same artifact, and all SQL lives behind tools._conn() against one claims database.
findings.gap: The two deployables share one artifact, one database credential (claims/db/readwrite), and one IAM role (claims-agent-execution), so they are not independently deployable or independently privileged. docs/security-review-TODO.md notes the consequence: a tool compromise gets the agent's model and memory permissions too.
findings.recommendation: Keep the modular structure - it is working - but split the deployment identity: separate execution roles for the runtime and the tool Lambda, and separate database credentials scoped to the SQL each actually issues (read-only for policy_lookup/payment_history, write for settlement_writer). Further decomposition is not warranted at this size.

findings.title: All inter-service communication synchronous across four downstream dependencies
findings.description: Every outbound call in the triage path is synchronous and blocking: agent_rt.retrieve (retrieval.py), agentcore.retrieve_memory_records (memory.py), bedrock.converse (agent.py), each tool's psycopg2 round trip (tools.py), then agentcore.create_event. No message publication, no event emission on settlement, no queue consumer, no Lambda event source mapping.
findings.gap: Archetype anti-pattern: for an orchestrator, synchronous-only fan-out across 3+ dependencies scores 1 - cascading failure risk and timeout amplification are structural. This calibration is what distinguishes the score from a data-gateway or stateless-utility, where identical sync-only evidence would be the correct design.
findings.recommendation: Make the settlement decision an event (EventBridge) rather than an inline database write plus payment-queue insert, and move claim intake onto a queue so a Bedrock or database stall does not hold the caller open. Retain synchronous calls for the model invocation and the policy/payment reads, where request/response is appropriate.

findings.title: No async job surface, status polling, or checkpointing for long-running batch triage
findings.description: There is no asynchronous job surface, no status API, and no checkpointing. triage() holds the caller for the full retrieve, recall, model, tool, persist sequence. docs/batch-mode.md processes up to 500 claims in a single invocation with no per-claim checkpoint, so an interruption leaves an unknown subset settled and paid, recoverable only by manually reversing payment_queue rows. The tool Lambda's Timeout: 60 bounds individual tool calls but nothing bounds or resumes the overall coordination.
findings.gap: Archetype-calibrated: for an orchestrator, the rubric's score-1 case is 'all long-running coordination synchronous - caller must hold connection open', which is exactly the observed design. A stateless-utility with no operations exceeding 30 seconds would instead have been recorded as Not Evaluated.
findings.recommendation: Convert batch triage to one durable execution per claim (Step Functions driven by a queue) with persisted per-claim state so progress is checkpointed, retries are idempotent, and a run can resume rather than be unwound by hand. Expose run status instead of holding the connection open.

findings.title: MCP tool contract is unversioned and advertises empty input schemas
findings.description: The service's contract is the MCP tool surface in tools.REGISTRY - load_claim, policy_lookup, payment_history, settlement_writer. Tool names carry no version, the gateway declares no stage or version, and _tool_specs() in agent.py advertises an empty input schema ({'type':'object','properties':{}}) for every tool, so there is no declared contract to version. No OpenAPI, AsyncAPI, or GraphQL specification exists, and no changelog.
findings.gap: No versioning on a tool contract whose consumers include a model that selects tools by name and schema. Any rename or semantic change to settlement_writer breaks every caller simultaneously with no compatibility window, and the empty input schemas make argument changes invisible to consumers today.
findings.recommendation: Publish real JSON Schemas per tool (replacing the empty properties stub), version the tool contract explicitly (versioned tool names or a gateway stage), keep the prior version serving while consumers migrate, and maintain a changelog for the tool surface.

findings.title: Endpoints resolved via SSM and environment variables with no dynamic discovery
findings.description: Endpoints are resolved through configuration, not discovery. infra/agent-runtime.yaml uses SSM Parameter Store indirection at deploy time ({{resolve:ssm:/claims/tool-endpoint}}, /claims/kb-id, /claims/artifact-bucket), and the application reads CLAIMS_MEMORY_ID, CLAIMS_KB_ID, CLAIMS_MODEL_ID, and CLAIMS_DB_SECRET from environment variables. No AWS Cloud Map, service mesh, or dynamic registry; SSM values resolve once at stack deploy, so a dependency relocation requires a redeploy.
findings.gap: Externalized configuration without dynamic discovery - better than hard-coded literals, but endpoint changes are deployment-coupled.
findings.recommendation: Parameter-store indirection is adequate at this service count; if the tool surface grows into multiple independently-deployed targets, move to AWS Cloud Map so targets resolve at call time. Prefer stack outputs and cross-stack references over loose SSM paths so each dependency is typed and its producer identifiable.

findings.title: Managed vector store in place but ingestion pipeline undeclared and retrieval unscoped
findings.description: The unstructured corpus - free-text claim descriptions and the prior-claims archive - lives in managed stores. src/claims_agent/retrieval.py documents a Bedrock knowledge base backed by an OpenSearch Serverless vector collection whose ingestion loads the full claims archive including closed and denied claims. No automated parsing or extraction pipeline exists: no Textract, no Tika, no PDF/image library in requirements.txt, no chunking or loader code. Neither the knowledge base nor its S3 data source is defined in this repo's IaC.
findings.gap: Managed vector storage is in place but the ingestion and extraction path is undeclared and unparameterized - notably its scope. docs/security-review-TODO.md records that the knowledge base holds the entire claims archive with no per-principal filter so retrieval can surface another claimant's record into a prompt, and retrieval.py issues retrieve with only numberOfResults and no metadata filter.
findings.recommendation: Declare the knowledge base, its S3 data source, and the ingestion job in IaC, attach a parsing/metadata-extraction step so each ingested claim carries claimant and policy attributes, then apply a metadata filter on retrieve so retrieval is scoped to the claim under triage rather than the whole archive.

findings.title: Single connection factory but inline per-tool SQL and a second unrelated read path
findings.description: Relational access is centralized: every tool in src/claims_agent/tools.py obtains its connection from the single _conn() helper, the one place credentials are fetched and a connection constructed. All queries are parameterized (%s placeholders) with no string interpolation into SQL. But raw SQL is inlined per tool function with no repository or DAO abstraction, there is no ORM, and the knowledge-base read path in retrieval.py is a separate client over the same claims corpus with no shared contract.
findings.gap: One connection factory but four independent inline SQL statements plus a second unrelated retrieval path. Schema changes require edits scattered across tool functions, and the two read paths over claims data can diverge in what they consider visible.
findings.recommendation: Introduce a thin repository layer per entity (claims, policies, payments) so SQL and row mapping live in one place per table, and route both the SQL and knowledge-base read paths through a common claims-access contract so visibility rules are enforced once.

findings.title: Database engine version unpinned and EOL status unknown from in-repo evidence
findings.description: No database engine version is pinned anywhere. The claims database is PostgreSQL by inference only (psycopg2-binary>=2.9.9 in requirements.txt), with no EngineVersion property, no Compose or Helm engine tag, and no migration tooling recording a target version. Other runtime versions are pinned (Runtime: python3.12 on the tool Lambda), and AgentCore Memory is managed with no customer-managed engine version, so the gap is confined to the relational engine. No version-update procedure is documented.
findings.gap: Engine version and EOL status are unknown from in-repo evidence: some versions are pinned, the database engine is implicit, and there is no documented upgrade, downtime, or rollback procedure for it.
findings.recommendation: Pin the claims database engine version explicitly wherever the instance is declared, record the version and its EOL date alongside the service, and document the version-update procedure (downtime window, rollback, risk acceptance) so engine currency is tracked rather than inferred from a driver pin.

findings.title: No KMS or encryption-at-rest configuration on memory, transcript logs, or claims data
findings.description: No encryption-at-rest configuration exists on any data surface. Searched and not found across both templates: AWS::KMS::Key, any KmsKeyId/KmsMasterKeyId, and any kms: action in the execution-role policies. The three at-rest surfaces are all unencrypted-by-configuration: ClaimsMemory (which per memory.py persists the raw exchange, and per docs/security-review-TODO.md includes claimant SSN and bank routing numbers with nothing redacting before the write); ClaimsTranscriptLogs with RetentionInDays 3653 holding full prompts and completions logged at INFO by agent.py; and the claims database storing claimant_ssn and routing_no.
findings.gap: Highly sensitive personal and financial data - SSNs, bank routing numbers, and complete model prompts containing both - is retained for up to ten years with no customer-managed key, no key policy, no rotation, and no data-protection policy on the log group. There is no key boundary to revoke if the single shared execution role is compromised.
findings.recommendation: Create a customer-managed KMS key for the claims workload with a key policy scoped to the service roles and a documented rotation policy, and apply it to the Memory store, the transcript log group, and the claims database. Independently, stop writing SSNs and routing numbers into memory and logs: redact before the Memory write and remove the full prompt/completion log.info calls in agent.py, or attach a CloudWatch Logs data-protection policy. Reduce the 3653-day retention to what is actually required.

findings.title: Tool gateway is unauthenticated and the runtime is directly invocable account-wide
findings.description: The tool endpoint is unauthenticated. ClaimsToolGateway declares AuthorizerType: NONE; there is no Cognito user pool, no JWT or OIDC authorizer, no API key, and no auth middleware in the application - tools.dispatch is the Lambda handler with no caller validation, and tools.REGISTRY is invoked by name directly from the model's toolUse block. docs/security-review-TODO.md confirms both the gateway position ('anyone who can reach the endpoint can call any tool') and a second unmediated path (the runtime ARN accepts SigV4 from any principal in the account, so gateway-side controls are advisory).
findings.gap: No per-request authentication on an endpoint that exposes settlement_writer - a tool that marks claims settled and inserts into payment_queue. Calls are neither authorized nor attributable, so a settlement cannot be traced to a principal, and the documented compensating control (network reachability) is itself absent.
findings.recommendation: Attach a JWT/OIDC authorizer to the gateway so every tool call carries a verifiable caller identity, propagate that identity into tool execution, and authorize per tool so only entitled principals can reach settlement_writer. Close the direct-SigV4 path with a resource policy so the authenticated gateway is the only entry point.

findings.title: No identity provider integration; actor identity is an unverified CLI argument
findings.description: No identity-provider integration exists. Searched and not found: AWS::Cognito::*, any OIDC or SAML configuration, any federation or SSO setting, and any identity library in requirements.txt. The only identity concept in the application is --actor-id, a free-text CLI argument defaulting to the shared literal 'adjuster-pool' in src/claims_agent/agent.py, passed straight into memory reads and writes as the actor key. Nothing verifies it.
findings.gap: The service manages no authentication at all and federates with nothing; the actor identity that scopes memory access is a caller-supplied, unverified string with a shared default. Per-claimant or per-adjuster access decisions are therefore impossible, which also underpins the shared memory namespace recorded in docs/security-review-TODO.md.
findings.recommendation: Integrate with the organization's centralized IdP (Cognito federating to the corporate provider, or the provider directly) so adjuster identity arrives as a verified token claim, and derive actor_id from that claim rather than a CLI argument. This is a prerequisite for per-actor memory partitioning and per-principal retrieval scoping.

findings.title: Secrets Manager used with no plaintext credentials, but no rotation and a wildcard grant
findings.description: Production credentials are in AWS Secrets Manager and retrieved at runtime: src/claims_agent/tools.py calls secretsmanager.get_secret_value(SecretId=_SECRET) and parses host/username/password from the result. No plaintext credentials are present anywhere in the repository - no .env, no application.properties, no password literal in code or IaC, no credential embedded in a connection string. docs/security-review-TODO.md records the migration out of environment variables as closed, consistent with the code.
findings.gap: No rotation is configured: the secret is not declared in this repo's IaC, so there is no AWS::SecretsManager::RotationSchedule or rotation Lambda, and the name claims/db/readwrite indicates a single read-write credential shared by all four tools. The grant is also unscoped - secretsmanager:GetSecretValue on Resource '*' in infra/agent-iam.yaml - so the role can read every secret in the account.
findings.recommendation: Declare the secret in IaC with an automated rotation schedule, split it into least-privilege credentials (read-only for the lookup tools, write-capable only for settlement_writer), and scope the IAM grant to those specific secret ARNs instead of '*'.

findings.title: No patching automation, vulnerability scanning, or image/dependency pinning
findings.description: No patching or vulnerability-management mechanism is present. Searched and not found: .github/dependabot.yml or .yaml, renovate.json, .renovaterc*, any .snyk policy, any SSM patch baseline, any Amazon Inspector configuration, and any ECR image-scanning setting. There is no Dockerfile in the repository, so the base image is not visible or pinnable here, and the runtime consumes the mutable tag claims-agent:latest. requirements.txt uses open lower bounds with no lockfile, so the installed dependency set is not reproducible. docs/security-review-TODO.md claims digest pinning in prod was done in April, which infra/agent-runtime.yaml contradicts.
findings.gap: No evidence of a patching strategy and no vulnerability scanning, on a container with an unpinned base image and unpinned Python dependencies. The documented digest pinning is not reflected in the template that actually deploys the runtime.
findings.recommendation: Pin ContainerUri to an image digest and make the ECR repository immutable with scan-on-push; enable Amazon Inspector for the container and Lambda; add Dependabot or Renovate at a canonical path with a compiled, pinned lockfile so transitive CVEs surface as reviewable changes. Reconcile the template with the digest-pinning claim in the security review.

findings.title: No SAST, dependency, container, or agent-safety scanning before release
findings.description: There is no pipeline and therefore no pipeline security validation. Searched and not found: any SAST configuration (SonarQube, Semgrep, CodeGuru), any dependency-scanning step (pip-audit, safety, Dependabot config), any container scanning, and any .snyk file. docs/security-review-TODO.md states the position directly: releases are promoted on unit tests only, with no safety or tool-correctness evaluation before deploy.
findings.gap: No security validation step of any kind before release, on a service that handles SSNs and releases payments. No agent-specific safety gate exists either - docs/security-review-TODO.md records that no Bedrock guardrail is attached and that a prompt-injection test against the claimant-controlled description field has never been run, even though that field flows straight into the model prompt via retrieval.similar_claims(claim['description']) and the prompt payload in agent.py.
findings.recommendation: Add SAST plus dependency and container scanning to the pipeline as gates that block on critical findings. Given the workload, add an evaluation gate alongside them: prompt-injection tests against claimant-controlled fields, tool-correctness checks on settlement_writer, and a Bedrock guardrail attached to the invocation path so release safety is verified rather than assumed.

findings.title: No distributed tracing or correlation across the four boundaries each triage pass crosses
findings.description: No tracing instrumentation exists. requirements.txt contains no OpenTelemetry or aws-xray-sdk dependency; no TracingConfig is set on the tool Lambda; no traceparent or X-Amzn-Trace-Id propagation appears in the code. Observability is limited to unstructured logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO) with a bare '%(asctime)s %(message)s' format - no correlation ID, session ID, or claim ID in a structured field. docs/security-review-TODO.md confirms the consequence: an end-to-end agent session cannot be reconstructed across gateway, runtime, and memory when an adjuster disputes a recommendation.
findings.gap: No trace propagation across the four service boundaries the agent crosses per triage pass, and no correlation key tying gateway invocation, model call, tool execution, and memory write into one session. A disputed settlement cannot be reconstructed.
findings.recommendation: Instrument with OpenTelemetry (or X-Ray via TracingConfig: Active on the Lambda plus the SDK in the runtime), propagate a session/trace identifier from the gateway through tool dispatch into the memory write, and emit structured JSON logs carrying trace ID, session ID, actor ID, and claim ID so a single triage pass is queryable end to end.

findings.title: No SLOs, alarms, or threshold definitions for the triage journey
findings.description: No monitoring artifact of any kind exists in the repository. Searched and not found: any AWS::CloudWatch::Alarm, any dashboard definition, any latency or error-rate threshold, and any SLO or error-budget declaration in code, config, or docs. infra/agent-runtime.yaml provisions a log group but no alarm on it. Because there are no threshold-based alarms at all, the scoring guidance's Score-2 floor (alarms implying implicit SLOs) does not apply.
findings.gap: No definition of acceptable service levels for the triage path - no target for triage latency, tool error rate, or model-invocation failure - so degradation is undetectable and there is no basis for prioritizing the operational gaps in this report.
findings.recommendation: Define SLOs for the adjuster-facing triage journey (p95 triage latency, tool error rate, settlement-write success rate), implement them as CloudWatch alarms in IaC, and track an error budget. Note that SLO tooling frequently lives in an external monitoring platform; this score reflects only what is observable in the repository.

findings.title: No business metrics on settlement volume, value, or override rate
findings.description: No custom metrics are published. Searched and not found: any put_metric_data call, any embedded-metric-format emission, and any dashboard definition. The only instrumentation in src/claims_agent/agent.py is three log.info statements emitting the prompt, the completion, and each tool result as raw JSON - unqueryable as a metric and the source of the sensitive-data-in-logs problem. Settlement amounts recommended, auto-approval rate, adjuster override rate, tool failure rate, and batch payment volume are all unmeasured.
findings.gap: Only default platform metrics exist. For a service whose model recommends dollar amounts and whose batch mode releases payment without human review, there is no metric on settlement volume, value, or override rate - so a model regression that systematically over-approves would be invisible.
findings.recommendation: Publish business metrics for triage outcomes (recommendations issued, auto-approval rate, settled amount distribution, adjuster override rate, tool error rate by tool) and build a dashboard over them. Use embedded metric format from structured logs rather than logging raw prompt payloads.

findings.title: No alarms or anomaly detection on error rates, latency, or settlement volume
findings.description: No alerting is configured. Neither template defines a CloudWatch alarm, composite alarm, anomaly detector, SNS alarm topic, or any PagerDuty/OpsGenie integration, and no alert configuration exists in docs/. Nothing watches the model-invocation error rate, the tool failure rate, the payment_queue insert rate, or the nightly batch run.
findings.gap: No alerting at all - neither anomaly detection nor static thresholds. A failed or anomalous nightly batch run (up to 500 claims settled and paid without an adjuster) would be discovered only by someone noticing after the fact.
findings.recommendation: Add alarms on model and tool error rates, triage latency, and batch-run completion as a baseline, then layer CloudWatch anomaly detection on settlement volume and value so an unusual auto-approval pattern pages someone before payments are released. Route alarms to an on-call destination.

findings.title: Direct-to-production deployment on a mutable image tag with manual financial rollback
findings.description: Deployment is direct-to-production with no staged rollout. ClaimsAgentRuntime consumes ContainerUri '...claims-agent:latest' - a mutable tag, so a new image replaces the serving version wholesale on the next pull. Searched and not found: any CodeDeploy deployment configuration or appspec.yml, any Lambda alias, version, or traffic-shifting setting on ClaimsToolFunction, any weighted target group, and any feature-flag mechanism. docs/batch-mode.md describes the only rollback path in the repository, and it is manual and data-level: pull the payment_queue rows for the run and reverse them.
findings.gap: A prompt change, tool-schema change, or model change reaches 100% of auto-claims triage immediately, with no canary window and no automated rollback - and because settlements are written and payments released as a side effect, a bad release is not merely revertible code but financial transactions requiring manual reversal.
findings.recommendation: Deploy by immutable image digest through a staged rollout: publish a Lambda version and alias with CodeDeploy canary traffic shifting for the tool surface, and roll the runtime forward on a fraction of triage volume before full release, with automated rollback wired to error-rate alarms. Treat prompt and model-ID changes as deployments subject to the same gate.

findings.title: Two mocked happy-path unit tests; no integration coverage of the payment-releasing path
findings.description: The entire test suite is tests/test_tools.py - 23 lines, two tests, both unit-level with _conn patched to a MagicMock, self-described as 'Happy path only - no adversarial input cases yet.' test_settlement_writer_marks_settled asserts only the returned dict's status; it exercises no real SQL, so neither the UPDATE claims nor the INSERT INTO payment_queue statement is ever validated against a schema. Searched and not found: any integration or e2e test directory, test containers, contract tests, API test collections, and any CI configuration to run them. agent.py, memory.py, and retrieval.py have no tests at all.
findings.gap: No integration test covers the critical workflow - claim load, retrieval, model invocation, tool dispatch, settlement write, memory write - and nothing runs in a pipeline. The payment-releasing path has no end-to-end verification, no schema-drift detection, and no adversarial input coverage on the claimant-controlled description field.
findings.recommendation: Add an integration suite that runs the full triage path against an ephemeral Postgres and a stubbed Bedrock response, asserting the resulting claims and payment_queue rows; add contract tests for each MCP tool schema; and add adversarial cases for the claimant-controlled description field. Run all of it as a blocking pipeline stage.

findings.title: Incident response is one manual financial reversal plus ad hoc shell access
findings.description: One documented manual recovery procedure exists: docs/batch-mode.md states rollback is manual - pull the payment_queue rows for the run and reverse them. docs/security-review-TODO.md is an open-items register, not a runbook. No automation backs either: searched and not found - any SSM Automation document, any remediation Lambda, any Step Functions incident workflow, any self-healing pattern. The interactive bedrock-agentcore:InvokeAgentRuntimeCommandShell grant in infra/agent-iam.yaml is justified as on-call attaching to a live session, which is manual intervention by shell - and it is granted to the same role the agent and tools run under.
findings.gap: Incident response is documentation plus ad hoc shell access with no automation. The one procedure that exists is a hand-executed financial reversal with no idempotency guarantee, no record of what was reversed, and no scoping of which run's rows to touch.
findings.recommendation: Convert the batch rollback into an automated, auditable compensating action keyed to a run ID (an SSM Automation document or Step Functions workflow that reverses exactly the rows a given run inserted), and write machine-readable runbooks for common failure modes. Remove the CommandShell permission from the shared execution role and grant interactive access through a separate, auditable break-glass role.

findings.title: No CODEOWNERS, dashboards, or ownership attribution for observability assets
findings.description: No ownership metadata exists for any observability asset. Searched and not found: CODEOWNERS, any dashboard definition, any alarm with an owner, any SLO file with team attribution, and any team tag on a CloudWatch resource (no resource in either template carries tags at all). README.md names no owning team; docs/security-review-TODO.md refers to 'the platform team' as the raiser of findings but assigns no named owner to any of the fourteen open items.
findings.gap: There are no dashboards or alarms to own and no ownership attribution for the observability surface that does exist - the transcript log group. Monitoring is reactive and unassigned, and the open security register has no accountable owner per item.
findings.recommendation: Add a CODEOWNERS entry covering infra/ and the observability configuration, build a per-service dashboard owned by a named team, and tag alarms and log groups with that owner once alarms exist. Assign a named owner and target date to each open item in docs/security-review-TODO.md.

findings.title: Zero tags on all nine provisioned AWS resources
findings.description: Not a single resource in either CloudFormation template carries tags. Searched and not found: any Tags property on the AgentCore Runtime, Gateway, Gateway Target, Memory store, Lambda function, log group, or either IAM role; no stack-level tag convention documented; no required-tags Config rule and no Tag Policy. Resources are named consistently (claims-triage, claims-tools, claims-agent-execution) but a name is not a cost or ownership attribution.
findings.gap: Zero tag coverage across all nine provisioned resources. Cost of the agent workload - notably Bedrock model invocation and the 10-year transcript log group - cannot be allocated, resource ownership cannot be resolved during an incident, and environment cannot be distinguished.
findings.recommendation: Apply a consistent tag set (Owner, CostCenter, Environment, Application, DataClassification) to every resource in both templates, enforce it with AWS Config required-tags rules and Organizations Tag Policies, and activate the keys as cost allocation tags. DataClassification matters here specifically: it marks the Memory store and transcript log group as holding PII and financial data.

evaluations.title: Managed Compute
evaluations.reason: Score 4 - all compute managed: AWS::BedrockAgentCore::Runtime from a container image plus a python3.12 Lambda; no EC2 instance, launch template, or Auto Scaling group in either template.

evaluations.title: Programming Languages
evaluations.reason: Score 4 - Python 3.12 runtime with modern syntax and current SDK/framework set (boto3>=1.35.0, langchain-aws>=0.2.0, opensearch-py>=2.6.0); no language, framework, or SDK lag.

evaluations.title: Stored Procedures and Schema Complexity
evaluations.reason: Score 4 - no .sql files, no CREATE PROCEDURE/TRIGGER/FUNCTION, no T-SQL or PL/SQL; all four tools use portable parameterized ANSI SQL with business logic in the application and model layer.

evaluations.title: Audit Logging
evaluations.reason: Surface-gated: has_iac_provisioning_aws_resources=true but the IaC is application-scoped only (AgentCore Runtime/Gateway/Memory, tool Lambda, service log group, two service roles). No account/foundation-level resources (CloudTrail, Config, GuardDuty, SCPs, centralized log archive), which is the correct scope for an application repo. CloudTrail evaluation belongs in the foundation infrastructure repo.

scoring_notes: SEC: (1+1+1+3+1+1) / 6 = 8/6 = 1.33 - SEC-Q1 excluded (Not Evaluated, surface gate)
